You can use relative clauses to give more information about a noun. These are sometimes called adjective clauses as well.

A relative clause is a dependent clause and cannot be a complete sentence by itself.

There are two different types of Relative Clauses:

1. Defining Relative Clause: this contains information that is necessary to define or identify which particular noun you are talking about. You don't use commas with defining relative clauses:.

I asked the same question to my friend who I think is a great source of knowledge.

If you don't say “who I think is a great source of knowledge”, then we don't know which friend you are talking about.

2. Non-Defining Relative Clause: you use this to add extra information about a noun. This is not necessary to identify the noun. You need to put commas with non-defining relative clauses.

My friends just got back from a camping trip, which they said was awesome.

It is clear which camping trip you mean, so “which they said was awesome” is extra information.

Boris: Kristi and Adam, I wanted to let you both know that I read through your assignments, which were very well written, and am very pleased with your work. Congratulations!
Adam: Really? Phew, I thought I blew it!
Boris: Adam, if I wasn't confident in your abilities, I wouldn't have hired you. You are more than capable.
Adam:Thanks, Boris.
Boris: Keep up the good work.
Adam: Will do.

Boris: Kristi, you also did a fantastic job. Your biography, which I read twice, was well organized.
Kristi:Thank you. That means a lot.
Boris: It's refreshing to see some young talent in the office.
Adam: Boris, who is usually ill-mannered and sharp-tongued, is being rather sentimental today. Wouldn't you agree, Kristi?
Kristi: You're going to get us in trouble, Adam! You know that Boris, whose mood I don't want to spoil, doesn't like to be interrupted while he's talking.
Adam: He's not even looking at us! Let alone paying attention to us!
Kristi: Adam, your deduction skills are excellent! Well done!
Boris: Ms. Lenard, pay attention please. Now, I wanted to mention that there's a position within the company that's opened up.

Kristi: What is it?
Boris: The role, which includes more responsibilities than your current position, is one both of you are qualified for and would do well in. Essentially, the candidate that we hire should be analytical and diligent.
Adam: You mean someone who's a perfectionist? Kristi that sounds just like you! You have got to apply!
Kristi: Very funny, Adam.
Boris: Like I said, it's a position either of you would fare well in. I think both of you two, who are potential and strong candidates, should apply. Perhaps, I may even put in a good word for you guys. Here's a copy of the job description. Have a look.
